name: Russell's Viper
pattern: Three rows of dark oval spots ringed with black and white
keyFeatures: Flat triangular head with a V or X mark
Loud, long hiss when disturbed
Thick body with a short tail
behaviour: Slow moving but strikes very fast. Common around rice fields where rats gather, which makes it a leading cause of snakebite in farming areas.
description: One of Sri Lanka's most dangerous snakes and a major cause of serious snakebite among farmers.
biteSymptoms: Bleeding from gums or the wound

name: Indian Cobra
pattern: Plain or faintly banded body; many have a spectacle mark on the hood
keyFeatures: Spreads a broad hood when threatened
Smooth glossy scales
Spectacle or single-ring mark on the hood
behaviour: Raises its front body and spreads its hood as a warning. It usually retreats if given space and is often found near villages and rat holes.
description: A well-known venomous snake that spreads a hood when alarmed.
biteSymptoms: Pain and swelling at the bite

name: Common Krait
pattern: Glossy blue-black body with thin white cross-bands, often faint on the front half
keyFeatures: Raised ridge of enlarged scales along the back
Blunt head barely wider than the neck
Active at night and often found indoors
behaviour: Shy and slow-moving by day but dangerous at night. Bites often cause little pain, so victims may not realise how serious they are.
description: A small but deadly snake. Bites can happen while people sleep on the floor, and they may be almost painless.
biteSymptoms: Little or no pain at the bite

name: Ceylon Krait
pattern: Dark brown to black body with narrow white bands
keyFeatures: Narrow pale bands on a dark body
Blunt rounded head
Smooth shiny scales
behaviour: A secretive, nocturnal snake of the wet zone that hides under leaf litter and logs by day. It is rarely seen and not aggressive.
description: An endemic krait of the wet zone. Rarely encountered, but its bite is a medical emergency.

name: Saw-scaled Viper
pattern: Pale sandy body with a wavy pale line along each side and a cross mark on the head
keyFeatures: Small, stout body
Rubs its scales together to make a rasping sound
Cross or arrow mark on the head
behaviour: Irritable and quick to strike. Makes a distinctive sawing sound by rubbing its coiled body scales together before it bites.
description: A small, fast and irritable viper of the dry coastal regions.
biteSymptoms: Bleeding from the wound or gums

name: Hump-nosed Viper
pattern: Mottled brown, grey or tan with darker blotches that blend into leaf litter
keyFeatures: Upturned snout that gives a hump-nosed profile
Small and well camouflaged in leaf litter
Triangular head
behaviour: Lies motionless in leaf litter and is easily stepped on. Bites are common, especially in plantations, and need urgent hospital care.
description: A small but medically important viper. It causes many bites because it is so hard to see.

name: Green Pit Viper
pattern: Green to yellow-green body, often with dark cross-bands
keyFeatures: Triangular head with heat-sensing pits
Bright green body
Gripping tail used for climbing
behaviour: Rests coiled on branches and shrubs during the day. Rarely bites unless disturbed, and bites usually cause only local effects.
description: A bright green endemic viper of the hill country and wet zone.
biteSymptoms: Pain and swelling near the bite

name: Green Vine Snake
pattern: Slender bright green body with a long pointed snout
keyFeatures: Very slender body
Long pointed head with horizontal pupils
Camouflaged among leaves
behaviour: Moves slowly through bushes and sways like a vine. Rear-fanged and very rarely a danger to people.
description: A slender tree snake that blends perfectly into foliage.

name: Sri Lankan Cat Snake
pattern: Brown or tan body with darker cross-bands and a large head
keyFeatures: Large head distinct from a thin neck
Vertical slit-like pupils
Slim body, climbs trees at night
behaviour: A slim, nocturnal tree snake that hunts birds and lizards. Mildly venomous and not considered dangerous to people.
description: A night-active tree snake with a large head and slit-like pupils.

name: Sri Lankan Flying Snake
pattern: Green-black body with yellow-orange spots and black bands on the head
keyFeatures: Glides between trees by flattening its body
Slender and agile
Black bands across the head
behaviour: Flattens its body to glide short distances from tree to tree. Mildly venomous and harmless to people in practice.
description: A colourful tree snake famous for gliding between branches.

name: Dog-faced Water Snake
pattern: Grey-brown body with dark blotches that fade with age
keyFeatures: Upturned nostrils on a broad head
Lives in brackish water and mangroves
Heavy-bodied for its length
behaviour: Hunts fish in estuaries and lagoons. Bites are uncommon and mild.
description: A heavy-bodied snake of brackish water and mangroves.

name: Green Keelback
pattern: Olive-green body with fine dark and orange markings near the neck
keyFeatures: Keeled scales
Orange or yellow neck markings
Found near water and damp areas
behaviour: Feeds on frogs near ponds, streams and wet gardens. Rarely bites and has mild venom.
description: A small green water-edge snake that eats frogs.

name: Indian Python
pattern: Large irregular dark brown blotches on a tan or cream body
keyFeatures: Very large, heavy body
Heat-sensing pits along the upper lip
Spear-shaped mark on the head
behaviour: Kills prey by constriction. Protected by law in Sri Lanka and not a threat to people if left alone.
description: A large, harmless constrictor protected under Sri Lankan law.

name: Common Rat Snake
pattern: Brown to olive above, with darker scale edges towards the tail and a pale belly
keyFeatures: Long slender body with large eyes
Often raises its head high when threatened
Very fast moving
behaviour: Hunts rats and frogs. Often mistaken for a cobra, but it is harmless and helps farmers by controlling rodents.
description: A fast, harmless snake that is often mistaken for a cobra.

name: Common Wolf Snake
pattern: Brown to black body with thin pale cross-bands that fade towards the tail
keyFeatures: Flattened head with an indistinct neck
Thin pale bands on a dark body
Often found inside houses at night
behaviour: Eats lizards and geckos, so it often enters houses. Frequently killed by mistake because it looks like a krait.
description: A small harmless snake that is often confused with a krait.

name: Common Sand Boa
pattern: Brown blotches on a sandy body; short and thick
keyFeatures: Short blunt tail that resembles a head
Thick sturdy body
Burrows into loose soil
behaviour: Spends the day buried in loose soil. Harmless but often killed because it is mistaken for a viper.
description: A stout burrowing snake often mistaken for Russell's Viper.

name: Checkered Keelback
pattern: Olive-brown body with a checkered pattern of dark squares and a dark streak behind the eye
keyFeatures: Keeled scales
Checkered markings
Strong swimmer found near water
behaviour: Common in paddy fields, tanks and ditches, where it hunts frogs and fish. It may flatten its neck when scared.
description: A common water snake of paddy fields and tanks.

name: Trinket Snake
pattern: Brown body with dark stripes along the back and dark lines on the head
keyFeatures: Dark streaks behind the eye
Slim and quick
Striped pattern towards the tail
behaviour: Hunts rodents and lizards on the ground and in low bushes. Harmless to people.
description: A slim, fast-moving harmless snake of scrub and gardens.

name: Bronzeback Tree Snake
pattern: Bronze-brown above with pale stripes along the sides
keyFeatures: Slender body and large eyes
Bronze sheen on the back
Lives in trees and shrubs
behaviour: Fast and agile, it hunts lizards and frogs in bushes. It may puff its throat to look bigger when scared.
description: A quick, harmless tree snake with a bronze sheen.

name: Sri Lankan Shieldtail
pattern: Smooth, shiny, dark brown body, paler underneath
keyFeatures: Short pointed snout for burrowing
Flat shield-like tail tip
Rarely seen above ground
behaviour: A burrowing snake of the wet zone that lives in loose soil and feeds on earthworms. Completely harmless.
description: An endemic burrowing snake with a shield-shaped tail.

name: Brahminy Blind Snake
pattern: Shiny dark thread-like body that looks like an earthworm
keyFeatures: Tiny worm-like body
Eyes reduced to small dots
Tail ends in a tiny spine
behaviour: Lives in soil and under pots and stones, feeding on ants and termites. Often mistaken for an earthworm.
description: The smallest snake in most gardens, often mistaken for an earthworm.

name: Banded Kukri Snake
pattern: Brown body with pale cross-bands, often confused with a krait
keyFeatures: Pale cross-bands on a brown body
Wide curved rear teeth shaped like a kukri knife
Head only slightly wider than the neck
behaviour: Eats reptile eggs. Looks like a krait but is harmless, and it is often killed by mistake.
description: A harmless egg-eater that looks like a krait.

name: Lowland Hump-nosed Viper
venomType: Haemotoxic and cytotoxic; can cause bleeding problems and kidney injury
pattern: Brown or grey with darker blotches and a dark stripe running across the eye and cheek
keyFeatures: Snout tip turned up into a small wart-like hump
Flat triangular head with a heat-sensing pit between nostril and eye
Often rests with its head held at an angle to the ground
behaviour: Lies still in leaf litter, often in rubber, tea and cinnamon plantations and home gardens of the south-western wet zone. Most bites happen when people step on or reach near it.
description: A small endemic pit viper of the lowland wet zone. It has caused serious bleeding and kidney injury in Sri Lanka.
biteSymptoms: Pain, swelling and blistering at the bite
Bleeding from the bite or gums

name: Highland Hump-nosed Viper
venomType: Haemotoxic and cytotoxic; mostly local effects, but treat every bite as an emergency
pattern: Brown to grey with a row of darker blotches along each side
keyFeatures: Strongly upturned snout
Small, stout body with a short tail
Triangular head with a pit between nostril and eye
behaviour: A small, slow viper of the central hills. It hides among leaves and rocks on the forest floor and in forest edges, ambushing frogs and lizards at night.
description: The smallest of Sri Lanka's three hump-nosed vipers, found only in the hill country.
biteSymptoms: Pain and swelling at the bite

name: Hook-nosed Sea Snake
pattern: Grey to grey-green above with dark cross-bands, paler on the belly
keyFeatures: Flat paddle-shaped tail
Pointed, beak-like snout
Nostrils on top of the head
behaviour: Lives in shallow, muddy coastal water, lagoons and river mouths. It is often caught in fishing nets and may bite and hold on when handled. Fishermen are at greatest risk.
description: The sea snake most often met by Sri Lankan fishermen. Its venom is very potent.
biteSymptoms: Bite may be painless at first

name: Slender Coral Snake
venomType: Neurotoxic; bites are very rare but it is a true elapid, so treat it as dangerous
pattern: Plain brown body with a black head marked with pale spots and black rings on a short tail
keyFeatures: Very thin, pencil-like body
Black head with white or yellow spots
Shows the bright blue underside of its tail when disturbed
behaviour: A shy burrower that lives under leaf litter and logs. If disturbed it hides its head and curls its tail up to flash the coloured underside.
description: A tiny, secretive coral snake. Rarely seen, but its venom acts on the nerves.

name: Brown Vine Snake
pattern: Greyish brown, powdered with darker brown, with dark diagonal blotches and a dark stripe through the eye
keyFeatures: Extremely thin, whip-like body
Long pointed snout
Horizontal keyhole-shaped pupil
behaviour: Rests motionless in shrubs where it looks like a dry twig or vine. Opens its mouth wide as a warning display and hunts lizards by day.
description: A twig-like tree snake found only in Sri Lanka. Mildly venomous and not dangerous to people.

name: Ornate Flying Snake
pattern: Yellow-green body crossed by black bars, often with red or orange flower-like spots along the back
keyFeatures: Can glide between trees by flattening its body
Large eyes and a flat head
Ridges along the belly help it climb bark
behaviour: An agile climber that hunts geckos and lizards in trees and coconut palms. It launches itself from branches and glides to lower perches.
description: A colourful gliding snake, larger and more boldly marked than the Sri Lanka Flying Snake.

name: Forsten's Cat Snake
pattern: Brown or grey with dark zigzag cross-bars and a dark streak behind the eye
keyFeatures: Large head on a thin neck
Big eyes with vertical cat-like pupils
Very long, slightly flattened body
behaviour: Climbs trees and roofs at night hunting roosting birds, lizards and rodents. It strikes readily if cornered but its venom is weak.
description: Sri Lanka's largest cat snake. Often found in roofs and mistaken for a viper.

name: Sri Lanka Pipe Snake
pattern: Black net pattern enclosing two rows of reddish-brown spots; white belly marked with black
keyFeatures: Smooth, cylindrical body with a small head
Very short, blunt tail
Flattens and raises its tail to look like a second head
behaviour: Hides under stones, logs and leaf litter by day. At night it hunts other small snakes. When threatened it hides its head and waves its flattened tail.
description: A small, harmless pipe snake found only in Sri Lanka. Its Sinhala name means 'two-headed cobra'.

name: Wart Snake
pattern: Dark grey with pale cross-bands; loose, baggy skin
keyFeatures: Rough sandpaper-like skin of tiny granular scales
Loose, baggy body
Small eyes on top of the head
behaviour: Fully aquatic and almost helpless on land. Lives in mangroves, lagoons and shallow coastal water, feeding on fish and crabs. Often caught in nets with sea snakes.
description: A harmless aquatic snake with rough skin, often confused with venomous sea snakes.

name: Barred Wolf Snake
pattern: Black or dark brown with narrow white or yellow cross-bars that break into spots towards the tail
keyFeatures: Flattened head slightly wider than the neck
Narrow pale bars on a dark body
Small eyes
behaviour: A small night hunter of geckos and skinks in the dry zone. Harmless, but often killed because it is mistaken for a krait.
description: A small, harmless banded snake of the dry zone that mimics kraits.

name: Buff-striped Keelback
pattern: Olive-brown with two buff or yellow stripes along the body crossed by dark bars
keyFeatures: Two pale stripes running down the body
Keeled (ridged) scales
Flattens its neck to show bright skin when alarmed
behaviour: Active by day in fields and garden edges, especially after rain, hunting frogs and toads. Shy and quick to escape.
description: A common, harmless striped snake of paddy fields and grassland.

name: Olive Keelback
pattern: Plain olive-green or olive-brown above, with a pale or orange edge to the belly
keyFeatures: Nostrils set high on the snout
Plain, unpatterned back
Keeled scales
behaviour: A semi-aquatic snake of tanks, ponds and flooded paddy fields that feeds on frogs and small fish. Harmless and rarely bites.
description: A plain olive water snake common around tanks and paddy fields.
